applicable_when: The kernel concatenates two (256, 16384) FP32 tensors into a (256, 32768) output — a pure memory-copy workload. With XBLOCK=128 (4 warps/block, 512 bytes/block), each block issues very few memory requests. On H200 with 4800 GB/s peak HBM bandwidth, the GPU needs large in-flight memory transactions to hide the ~17.4-cycle L1TEX latency. Only 39.9% occupancy is achieved (vs 100% theoretical), and 71.94% of scheduler cycles have no eligible warp — both symptoms of insufficient memory-level parallelism per SM. Increasing XBLOCK to 1024–4096 and num_warps to 8–16 will: (1) issue more concurrent memory requests per block, (2) give the warp scheduler more warps to switch between while waiting on L1TEX, and (3) reduce grid launch overhead (65536 → ~8192 blocks at XBLOCK=1024). Autotuning lets the runtime pick the optimal configuration for this H200 hardware.

applicable_when: The kernel is a simple concatenation (fused_cat) of two (256,16384) float32 tensors. With XBLOCK=128, each thread processes exactly 1 float32 element per load/store, issuing narrow 32-bit memory transactions. This prevents the compiler from emitting 128-bit vectorized loads (LDG.128), which are 4x more bandwidth-efficient. The dominant stall is L1TEX scoreboard (78.6% of all stall cycles, 17.4 cycles avg), meaning warps are blocked waiting for individual narrow loads to return. Increasing XBLOCK to 1024 means each thread processes 8 elements, enabling the Triton compiler to emit vectorized 128-bit loads/stores (4 floats = 16 bytes per transaction). This also reduces the grid from 65536 to 8192 CTAs, cutting launch overhead, and gives the compiler a larger instruction window to pipeline memory operations and hide latency.

strategy_title: Persistent Kernel Loop Causes Massive Instruction Explosion
strategy_description: Converting a flat 65536-CTA grid to a persistent 132-CTA kernel with an inner while-loop caused a ~71x slowdown (45.89 µs → 3030 µs). The root cause was an instruction count explosion from 10.9M to 1.61B executed instructions — a 147x increase — because the grid launch in kernel_function was NOT updated to use 132 CTAs; it still launched 65536 CTAs (cdiv(xnumel, 128)), each of which then ran the full inner while-loop over all 16384 tiles, causing every element to be processed 65536 times instead of once. The persistent kernel pattern requires the grid size to be reduced to NUM_SMS (132) simultaneously with adding the inner loop — failing to do so creates a catastrophic work multiplication. Even though occupancy improved (34.5% → 99.2%) and L2 hit rate rose (50.6% → 93.8%), the sheer volume of redundant work dominated all other effects.
slow_pseudocode:
# BROKEN: grid still uses 65536 CTAs but kernel has inner loop over all tiles
@triton.jit
def kernel(in0, in1, out, xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    num_tiles = tl.cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK)  # 16384 tiles
    tile_id = tl.program_id(0)           # 0..65535
    while tile_id < num_tiles:           # each of 65536 CTAs loops over all 16384 tiles
        # process tile...
        tile_id += 132                   # stride by NUM_SMS=132

grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # BUG: still 65536 CTAs, not 132!
kernel[grid](in0, in1, out, xnumel, XBLOCK=128)
fast_pseudocode:
# CORRECT persistent kernel: grid must be reduced to NUM_SMS
NUM_SMS = 132
XBLOCK = 512
@triton.jit
def kernel(in0, in1, out, xnumel, num_tiles, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    tile_id = tl.program_id(0)  # 0..131
    while tile_id < num_tiles:  # each SM processes ~124 tiles
        # process tile...
        tile_id += NUM_SMS

num_tiles = triton.cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK)  # 16384
grid = (NUM_SMS,)  # 132 CTAs only!
kernel[grid](in0, in1, out, xnumel, num_tiles, XBLOCK=XBLOCK)
applicable_when: Never apply this specific broken pattern. The persistent kernel pattern itself is valid when: grid is correctly set to NUM_SMS CTAs, the inner loop strides by NUM_SMS, and num_tiles is passed as a runtime argument.
do_not_apply_when: Do NOT apply persistent kernel transformation if the grid launch site is not simultaneously updated to use NUM_SMS CTAs. If the grid remains at the original flat size (e.g., cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK_small)) while the kernel body contains an inner while-loop, every CTA will redundantly process all tiles, causing O(original_grid_size) work multiplication. Also avoid when the kernel already runs many waves per SM (31+ waves) — the persistent pattern provides minimal benefit over the flat launch in that regime.
framework_notes: In Triton, the persistent kernel pattern requires coordinated changes in TWO places: (1) the @triton.jit kernel body must use tl.program_id(0) as the initial tile_id and stride by NUM_SMS, AND (2) the grid passed to kernel[grid](...) must be (NUM_SMS,) not the original flat grid. The diff in this iteration correctly modified the kernel body but left grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),) = 65536 in kernel_function, causing the catastrophic work multiplication. The XBLOCK=128 passed at the call site also conflicted with the intended XBLOCK=512 tile size, further compounding the issue.

strategy_title: maxnreg Cap + evict_first Fails for Large-XBLOCK Cat Kernels
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=16 to autotune configs with large XBLOCK (1024–4096) and switching eviction_policy to 'evict_first' caused an 8% regression despite reducing warp stall cycles (15.7→9.9 cycles/instruction) and improving scheduler eligibility (64.9%→46.5% no-eligible). The root cause is that the compiler still allocated 24 registers/thread (up from 18 before), and total executed instructions nearly doubled (10.9M→19.7M) due to the larger XBLOCK tile index arithmetic — the instruction count increase outweighed the latency-hiding benefit. DRAM throughput actually fell (20.5%→16.8%), indicating the kernel became more compute-bound on index arithmetic rather than memory-bound. The evict_first change alone had no measurable positive effect since L1 hit rate was already 0% and L2 hit rate was unchanged (~50%).
applicable_when: Never: this combination of large XBLOCK autotune + maxnreg cap regressed in both iteration 1 (0.857x) and iteration 2 (0.858x) for this memory-bound pointwise cat kernel.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply maxnreg caps combined with large XBLOCK autotune configs to memory-bound pointwise kernels where the baseline already uses few registers (≤18/thread). The maxnreg cap does not reliably reduce actual register allocation when the compiler needs registers for wide-tile index arithmetic — the compiler may still use more registers than the cap (or spill), and the doubled instruction count from larger tiles negates any occupancy benefit. Also, switching eviction_policy from 'evict_last' to 'evict_first' has no measurable effect when L1 hit rate is already 0% — the cache is not being reused regardless of eviction policy.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg is a per-config hint to the compiler but does not guarantee the specified register count — the compiler may still allocate more (as seen here: maxnreg=16 but actual registers=24) or may spill to local memory. The eviction_policy parameter in tl.load is a cache hint only and does not affect correctness. For streaming workloads with 0% L1 hit rate, changing eviction_policy between 'evict_last' and 'evict_first' has negligible performance impact.
